clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive NBIA subtype caused by biallelic variants in PLA2G6, encoding a calcium-independent phospholipase A2
Spans a spectrum from classic infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy through atypical childhood forms to adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism
Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy presents in the first years with psychomotor regression, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and visual impairment with optic atrophy
Characteristic pathology is widespread axonal spheroids (dystrophic axonal swellings) throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems
Cerebellar atrophy is an early and prominent MRI feature, and brain iron accumulation in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra develops later, often not present at first imaging
Iron-sensitive MRI sequences help detect the later basal ganglia iron that classifies the disorder within the NBIA group
The adult-onset form can resemble idiopathic Parkinson disease with dystonia, cognitive decline, and neuropsychiatric features
Diagnosis is confirmed by PLA2G6 molecular testing supported by the imaging evolution; care is symptomatic
reference.pathophysiology: PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration arises from biallelic variants in PLA2G6, which encodes a calcium-independent phospholipase A2 that remodels membrane phospholipids and maintains membrane integrity. Loss of enzyme function disturbs phospholipid homeostasis and mitochondrial membrane maintenance, leading to lipid peroxidation and progressive axonal degeneration with the formation of dystrophic axonal spheroids. Over time secondary iron accumulates in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, placing the disorder within the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation spectrum, though early in the disease iron deposition may be absent.
additionalDifferentials: Other NBIA subtypes, especially PKAN and BPAN
Leukodystrophies with early regression and spasticity
Young-onset Parkinson disease and other genetic parkinsonism (for the adult form)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to show cerebellar atrophy and, with iron-sensitive sequences, later pallidal and nigral iron
PLA2G6 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Electrophysiology and nerve conduction studies reflecting axonal involvement
Ophthalmological assessment and electroretinography for optic atrophy and visual pathway involvement
Serum caeruloplasmin, copper, and ferritin to distinguish other NBIA subtypes and Wilson disease
redFlags: Rapid developmental regression with loss of vision and motor skills in an infant
Progressive bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk
Acute respiratory compromise from progressive neuromuscular weakness
reference.prognosis: The classic infantile form is relentlessly progressive, typically leading to severe disability and death in childhood, whereas atypical and adult-onset forms progress more slowly over years to decades. No disease-modifying therapy is currently available.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal early MRI when brain iron has not yet accumulated
Missing the early cerebellar atrophy that is often the first imaging clue
Attributing adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism to idiopathic Parkinson disease without considering a genetic cause
Overlooking the peripheral nervous system involvement when interpreting neurophysiology
management: Symptomatic treatment of dystonia and parkinsonism with a trial of levodopa, anticholinergics and baclofen, and botulinum toxin for focal dystonia
Antiepileptic drugs for seizures alongside spasticity management with physiotherapy and occupational therapy
Nutritional support with management of dysphagia and gastrostomy feeding as regression advances
Respiratory care and management of secretions in advanced disease
Low-vision support and ophthalmology input for optic atrophy
Multidisciplinary neurodisability care with early palliative involvement given the progressive course
Genetic counselling and carrier and family testing for this autosomal recessive PLA2G6 disorder
